findings.summary: Page 7 opens with an ERR-trap / strict-mode example whose every ingredient is only introduced on page 8.
findings.evidence: Page 7's first block: `set -Eeuo pipefail` / `trap 'echo "L$LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND"' ERR` / `false | true || true   # ERR fires` / `echo "${PIPESTATUS[0]}"  # 1`, with note "without `|| true`, -e aborts the script there" — while page 8 is the page that first says "`trap handler ERR` fires on a non-zero return", "`set -euo pipefail`: exit on error, unset var, pipe failure" and defines `$BASH_COMMAND` and `$LINENO`.
findings.fix: Move this code block (and its note) onto page 8, beside the "Strict Mode Triple" bullets. Open page 7 with the leftover interrupt material currently stranded at the top of page 8 ("Neighbours: HUP And TSTP"), which follows page 6 naturally.

findings.summary: In the "Real vs Pseudo" flowchart a horizontal connector rail is drawn straight through the INT, TERM and HUP node labels, making them read as struck-through text.
findings.evidence: A single horizontal line crosses the vertical centre of the three boxes labelled `INT`, `TERM`, `HUP`, passing over the glyphs rather than routing between the rows.
findings.fix: Route the edges from `kernel signals` / `bash pseudo` down to the lower row around the INT/TERM/HUP boxes (add vertical rank spacing or orthogonal routing with an offset rail), so no connector overlaps a node label.

findings.summary: The single-vs-double-quote rule — the handbook's headline claim — is taught only as abstract card text, with no code example showing the two trap lines.
findings.evidence: Page 2's "Quoting Decides When" is a cards diagram reading "\"double\"": "expands NOW", "freezes old value"; "'single'": "expands at fire", "sees final value" — no `trap` line appears; the page's only code block is about subshell traps (`( trap 'echo sub' EXIT; : )`). The caption sells the part on "why double quotes in a trap string freeze the wrong value".
findings.fix: Add a 3–4 line code block under that heading contrasting `tmp=; trap "rm -f $tmp" EXIT` (expands to `rm -f` now) with `trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT; tmp=$(mktemp)` (removes the real file), so the learner sees the failure instead of being told about it.

findings.summary: In the "Orphans And Grandchildren" flowchart a connector line runs through the "grandchild (alive)" node label, making it look struck through.
findings.evidence: The horizontal rail joining `child A` and `child B` passes across the middle of the text `grandchild (alive)` inside its box.
findings.fix: Increase the vertical gap between the child row and the grandchild node and route the joining rail above the grandchild box instead of across it.

findings.summary: Temp-file material is split across the page 4/5 boundary with the background-PID block wedged in between, so the learner leaves and re-enters the temp-file topic.
findings.evidence: Page 4 ("Temp Files: mktemp, Guards, and Unlink") ends with "Capture The PID Now" / "`cmd &` backgrounds; `$!` holds that PID", and page 5 ("Killing Children: Jobs, PIDs, Groups") opens with "On failure keep the dir: `[[ $rc -eq 0 ]] || echo \"kept: $tmpdir\"`", "`mkfifo` pipes need the same trap treatment", "Lock files: `flock` an fd that closes on exit".
findings.fix: Swap the two blocks: end page 4 with the keep-on-failure / mkfifo / flock bullets (they finish the temp-resource story), and start page 5 with the "Capture The PID Now" block, which is the entry point to jobs and PIDs.

findings.summary: The last code line in the "Why is exit 1 in an INT trap a lie?" answer is clipped by the right edge of its code block, cutting the final character off the comment.
findings.evidence: Line renders as `trap - INT; kill -INT "$$"   # true 13` with the trailing glyph sliced by the block border at the right margin; the intended text is `# true 130` (matching "check $? for 130" earlier on the same page).
findings.fix: Shorten the comment (e.g. `# true 130` on its own line, or drop the inline comment) or reduce the code font size / widen the block so the full line fits inside the padded box.
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: The page 7 example claims ERR fires for a command on the left of `||`, directly contradicting the rule table on page 8.
findings.evidence: Page 7: "false | true || true   # ERR fires" versus page 8's "Where ERR Stays Silent" table row ["`a && b` / `a || b`","no (left side)"].
findings.fix: Drop the `|| true` and show the pipeline on its own line so ERR genuinely fires (keeping the note that `-e` then aborts), or relabel the comment to "ERR suppressed — left operand of `||`" and use it as the exemption example.

findings.summary: "Foreground process group" carries the Ctrl-C story from page 1 onward but is never defined until the `set -m` callout on page 5.
findings.evidence: Page 1 sidebox: "Terminal Ctrl-C: goes to the whole group" / "`kill -INT $$`: goes to your shell only"; page 2: "Ctrl-C hits the whole foreground process group"; the first explanation is page 5's callout, "A script launched from an interactive shell is already a group leader (`$$` == PGID)".
findings.fix: Add one bullet to page 1's signal section: "A process group is a set of related processes sharing a PGID; the terminal delivers Ctrl-C to every member of the foreground group at once."

findings.summary: `set -E` and `set -T` are cited as the fix for subshell trap loss with no gloss, and `set -T` is never explained in this part.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "ERR/DEBUG/RETURN skip subshells unless `set -E`/`set -T`". Page 8 later defines `set -E` ("By default ERR is not inherited by functions, command substitutions, or subshells. `set -E` fixes exactly that.") but `set -T` appears nowhere else in the content.
findings.fix: Expand the page 2 bullet to "`set -E` (errtrace) / `set -T` (functrace) — see page 8", and add a `set -T` line to page 8's errtrace callout.

findings.summary: `set -e` is load-bearing on pages 3–4 but its semantics are not taught until page 8.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "Normal end of script, explicit `exit`, `set -e` abort" and "`set -e` mid-cleanup can skip the rest of teardown"; page 4 sidebox: "`set -u` will not save you inside a trap string". Page 8 is the first place either is explained: "`set -euo pipefail`: exit on error, unset var, pipe failure".
findings.fix: Gloss the flag at first use on page 3 — e.g. "`set -e` abort (exit-on-error; full rules page 8)" — and add "(unset-variable check)" to the page 4 `set -u` mention.

findings.summary: The "Ans→" marker beside the question block is rendered at a size too small to be legible.
findings.evidence: The label `Ans→` under "Does an EXIT trap in a subshell run?" is roughly 8px tall against ~24px body text; the same marker recurs on page 6 under "Why is exit 1 in an INT trap a lie?".
findings.fix: Raise the answer-marker font size to at least ~60% of body text, or drop the marker and rely on the indented answer block.

findings.summary: `PIPESTATUS` is used in a code example but never defined anywhere in the part.
findings.evidence: Page 7: "echo \"${PIPESTATUS[0]}\"  # 1"; page 8's stack-trace table lists only `$?`, `$BASH_COMMAND`, `$LINENO`, `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}`, `${FUNCNAME[@]}`, and the strict-mode bullets mention pipefail but not `PIPESTATUS`.
findings.fix: Add a row or bullet on page 8: "`PIPESTATUS` — array of each pipeline element's status; read it immediately, the next command clobbers it", and keep the example with it.
